newsitem.title: GERMANY: German unions urge renewed effort on unemployment.
newsitem.headline: German unions urge renewed effort on unemployment.

text.p: Germany's top union official on Tuesday urged employers and government to work with unions to reduce unemployment as new data showed only a slight improvement in joblessness in March.

Opening a two-day jobs "summit", German Trade Union Federation (DGB) chairman Dieter Schulte warned of serious consequences if the attempt failed. He said government and business had missed a "great chance for cooperation" on job creation a year ago when the government-sponsored "Alliance for Jobs" idea collapsed.

Trade unions last year walked away from the jobs pact, which was designed to link job creation with modest wage demands, when the extent of the spending cuts in Bonn's current austerity package started to become known.
Hinting that the DGB and its member trade unions would be ready for a second attempt at cooperation with employers and politicians, Schulte said that a mood of "give and take" was now required.
"People must be able to feel that we are behaving honestly with each other," he said.
Schulte said current policies, including Bonn's programme of major tax reforms, could lead to Germany being ruled out of the single European currency in 1999.

"The complete removal of the means tax and lower corporate taxes, together with increased expenditure linked to greater joblessness and poverty, will lead to a rise in deficits up to the year 2000," Schulte said.
Bonn's official estimate is that its deficit will fall to 2.9 percent of economic output by year-end, just under the three percent ceiling for European monetary union (EMU).
The means tax was eliminated at the start of this year by order of Germany's highest court, a move opposed by Social Democrats who said it was giving a tax break to the well-off.
Schulte's critical sentiments were echoed by Dieter Hundt, who as president of the German Employers Federation usually sits on the opposite side of the bargaining table.

Hundt said blame for Germany's stubbornly high unemployment levels resides largely with Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government. The government had in particular gone back on promises made last year to lower the high social security costs faced by employers when taking on staff, he said.
"These promises have not been fulfilled in the last 14 months," Hundt told German radio, referring to the failed "Alliance for Jobs" pact.

The German Federal Labour Office said earlier on Tuesday that unemployment slipped by 15,000 to a seasonally adjusted 4.30 million in March. February data were also revised to show a decline in joblessness, the first since April 1996.
Despite the fall, the labour office said there was little sign that the economy was creating new jobs.

Rudolf Scharping, parliamentary leader of the opposition Social Democrats, told the conference the unemployment data indicated that all the government's budget data for this year were skewed, and he predicted the May tax estimate would show much larger revenue shortfalls than expected.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, at a bank opening in Berlin, acknowleged for the first time that average jobless levels in 1997 could exceed the government's previous forecast of 4.2 million, but he said the current labour market developments would not have a direct impact on the timetable for Europe's planned single currency.

Waigel said stubbornly high German unemployment levels would affect the federal budget but that there would be "no direct influence on the timetable for introducing the euro," Europe's planned single currency.
"We cannot rule out that unemployment levels will be higher than stated in the (government's) annual economic report," he said.

Leading trade union officials joined Schulte and Hundt in criticism of the Kohl government, with Klaus Zwickel, head of the mighty IG Metall trade union, saying that Bonn's current policies would not bring about the hoped-for reduction in joblessness over the next few years.
Speaking on German radio, the metal and engineering union chief said the government's goal of cutting unemployment in half by the year 2000 was "in no way achievable" at the current rate.
